solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Nice do spoilt by liquor having bad taste?

indicators.note: something spoilt is ruined and messed about, so the letters of the two words before it are jumbled

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a kind of liquor

explanation.surface: A party in Nice is ruined by someone bringing drink, which is in poor taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoilt' looks like it describes the party, but it signals the anagram; 'Nice' is the French city only in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecorum is improper behaviour, a lapse of good manners or propriety.

clue.text: Those bragging about, primarily, big feet?

indicators.note: the boasters' word goes around the other piece, embracing it

parts.note: boasters keep saying 'I am ...', so they are fancifully called I AMs

indicators.note: primarily signals that only the first letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A question about whether show-offs have large feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the B from 'primarily, big' inside IAMS, the plural of the boaster's 'I am'.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry an iamb is a metrical foot of one short and one long syllable.

clue.text: PC turned up positioned outside entrance of The Grand

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the built letters are read from the bottom upward
the word for positioned goes around the other letters

parts.note: posed means positioned, as a model is placed

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a grand is a thousand, abbreviated K

explanation.surface: A computer is carried upstairs and set up outside the entrance of a hotel called The Grand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts T (from 'entrance of The') and K inside POSED to make POTKSED; 'turned up' reads that backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A desktop is a personal computer designed to sit on a desk, one kind of PC.

clue.text: Slippery oil patch next to a little banger

indicators.note: slippery things slide about, so the letters of oil patch slide into a new order

explanation.surface: A car skids on a greasy patch of road beside a small, noisy old vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery' rearranges OIL PATCH into CHIPOLAT, then A is added. A banger is British slang for a sausage, as well as for an old car.
explanation.definitionFit: A chipolata is a small thin sausage, and a banger is British slang for a sausage.

clue.text: Official men with a right to tour medium-sized borstal

indicators.note: to tour is to travel around, so the long string goes around the small piece

parts.note: a referee, REF, is a match official
OR, other ranks, are ordinary soldiers or men
a Tory is a member of the political right
M is the clothing-size abbreviation for medium

explanation.surface: An official and his team, joined by a right-winger, inspect a mid-sized youth prison.
explanation.walkthrough: A borstal was a British prison for young offenders, abolished in 1982.
explanation.definitionFit: A reformatory is an institution for reforming young offenders, which is what a British borstal was.

clue.text: Old lady close to northern guy

parts.note: old lady is slang for mother, MA

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An elderly woman stands near a northern chap.
explanation.definitionFit: A guy is informal for a fellow or male person.

clue.text: One taken by small revolutionary security force

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
an exam taken is an exam sat

explanation.surface: Someone is captured by a small band of rebel security guards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' reads I + SAT + S backwards. 'revolutionary' seems to describe the force, but it only turns the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stasi was the state security police of communist East Germany.

clue.text: Don't slouch in places one enters heading north

indicators.note: in a down clue, heading north means read from the bottom upward
one goes into the word for places

parts.note: to place something is to put it, so places gives puts
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Advice to straighten up at places where someone walks in heading north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enters' puts I into PUTS to make PUTIS; 'heading north' reads it backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit up is to hold an upright posture, the opposite of slouching.

clue.text: Where one sees lots of fighting around uni

indicators.note: the word for fighting goes around the other letter

parts.note: soldiers in action are fighting
U is short for university, a uni

explanation.surface: Somewhere a lot of brawling breaks out near a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' puts U inside ACTION. 'lots of fighting' reads as one phrase, but the definition ends at 'lots', items for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Items at a sale by bidding are called lots, so an auction is where they are seen.

clue.text: Individuals entering the country, one in Asia

indicators.note: the individuals go into the word for the country

parts.note: India is the country, as the rest of the clue confirms by placing it in Asia
individuals are single ones

explanation.surface: People arriving in a country, one in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the country' alone could be anywhere; the phrase after it points to the Asian nation used as the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Indonesia is a nation of islands in south-east Asia, one of that continent's countries.

clue.text: Widespread argument broadcast on radio and Watchdog

indicators.note: radio listeners only hear words, so what is heard stands for the entry

parts.note: widespread means mass, as in mass appeal; a tiff is a petty quarrel or argument

explanation.surface: A broad dispute aired on radio and on the consumer television programme Watchdog.
explanation.walkthrough: MASS TIFF said out loud matches the dog. Watchdog is also a BBC consumer affairs television programme, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: A mastiff is a large, powerful dog breed traditionally kept to guard property.

clue.text: Saw how folk allergic to topping like their cake?

definitions.text: how folk allergic to topping like their cake?
definitions.meaning: people allergic to icing want their cake without it

explanation.surface: Someone observed how people who react to frosting prefer their cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Saw in the sense of observed or spotted; read as two words, it describes a cake with no icing.

clue.text: Ostentation regularly creates conflict

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, here every second one

explanation.surface: Showing off tends to cause fights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th and 10th letters of Ostentation.
explanation.definitionFit: A set-to is a brief fight or heated argument, a conflict.

clue.text: Function room

definitions.meaning: a function is a formal party or social event
the area in a hotel or office where visitors are greeted

explanation.surface: A space set aside for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal party, such as after a wedding, and also the front desk area of a hotel.

clue.text: Angry soldiers breaking up support for Jesus?

parts.note: cross means angry

indicators.note: the soldiers break into the word for support, splitting it

parts.note: to bear is to support a weight
RE is the Royal Engineers, British army soldiers

explanation.surface: Furious troops disrupt a show of support for Jesus.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: Simon of Cyrene carried the cross for Jesus. RE, the Royal Engineers, is a standard crossword source for soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-bearer carries the crucifix, as Simon of Cyrene did on the way to Calvary.

clue.text: Little drink of lager knocked back (not large)

indicators.note: not means leave out the following letter
knocked back means the word is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: Pils, short for Pilsner, is a pale lager
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A small taste of beer is downed, but not a big one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' turns PILS into SLIP, and 'not' drops the L. 'knocked back' suggests drinking, but it means reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A sip is a small mouthful of a drink.

clue.text: Celebrity panel situated on the right?

parts.note: a celebrity is a star
a board is a panel, of directors or of wood

explanation.surface: A panel of famous people sitting on the right-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the right is that of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, the starboard side is the right as one faces forward.

clue.text: Very thin stock made in part from this?

definitions.meaning: an idiom for someone extremely skinny

definitions.text: stock made in part from this?
definitions.meaning: soup stock is made by simmering bones, which might come in a sack

explanation.surface: A question about what goes into a thin broth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a skinny person; literally, a sack of bones is what a cook boils for stock.

clue.text: Light breeze in Anchorage heading from out west

parts.note: a bay is a sheltered place to anchor
a breeze is a light wind

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: W is the compass abbreviation for west

explanation.surface: A gentle breeze blows in the Alaskan city of Anchorage from the west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like an adjective for the breeze, but it is the definition. Anchorage reads as the city in Alaska but means a bay.
explanation.definitionFit: A light is a window, and a bay window is one that projects outward from a wall.

clue.text: You all moan oddly about son in an odd way

indicators.note: the reshuffled letters go around the following letter
oddly means in a strange arrangement, so the three words' letters are reshuffled

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Everyone grumbles strangely about a boy, which is itself strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges YOU ALL MOAN into ANOMALOULY, and 'about' puts S inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Anomalously means irregularly, deviating from what is normal or expected.

clue.text: Request to support side of batsman awaiting delivery?

indicators.note: in a down clue, the supporting word sits beneath the other

parts.note: in cricket the on side, or leg side, is the half of the field behind the batsman's legs
an order is a request for goods

explanation.surface: A plea to back the batsman's side while waiting for the bowler.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a delivery is a ball bowled to the batsman, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods on order have been requested but not yet arrived; the question mark marks the cricket pun.

clue.text: Drink daily, but not the ultimate in beer

indicators.note: but not signals leaving out the letter that follows

parts.note: a daily, or char, is a British cleaning woman who comes in each day

indicators.note: the ultimate in a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Having a drink every day, though not the final beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' removes R, from 'the ultimate in beer', from CHAR. 'daily' looks like an adverb but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Cha is an informal British word for tea, a hot drink.

clue.text: Clubs playing as well as they can in match?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, a card suit

parts.words: playing as well as they can
parts.note: players at their best are on form

explanation.surface: Golf or football clubs at their best during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' reads as a game, but it is a verb meaning agree.
explanation.definitionFit: To conform is to comply or fit in, to match a standard.

clue.text: A, perhaps, novel by old poet

indicators.note: novel means new, so the three words' letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Something rated A, maybe a novel written by a poet of old.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A is one of the human blood groups, alongside B, AB and O, so it exemplifies the answer.

clue.text: Dark inflatable boat husband's pushed out of

indicators.note: pushed out means removed from the word for the boat

parts.note: a dinghy is a small boat, often inflatable
H is the abbreviation for husband; the 's reads as 'is'

explanation.surface: A dark rubber boat that a husband was shoved out of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pushed out of' removes H from DINGHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingy means drab, gloomy and poorly lit.

clue.text: Private meal that comes without any starter

indicators.note: the first letter, the starter, is cut from the word for meal

parts.note: dinner is a main meal

explanation.surface: A private meal served with no first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without any starter' cuts D from DINNER; a starter is also a first course, which the surface plays on.
explanation.definitionFit: Inner means private or intimate, as in one's inner thoughts.

clue.text: Quantum particle found in serotonin

indicators.note: found in signals the letters sit inside the following word

explanation.surface: A tiny particle discovered within the brain chemical serotonin.
explanation.definitionFit: A roton is a quantum of rotational excitation in superfluid helium, a quasiparticle.

clue.text: Study by foremost of tasters in beer firm

indicators.note: the study and the letter go inside the word for beer

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
a den is a private room for study

indicators.note: the foremost of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A study of beer by the leading tasters at a brewing firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a company but is an adjective describing cooked pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: Al dente describes pasta cooked to remain slightly firm to the bite.

clue.text: I shot subordinate of Eisenhower at the front

indicators.note: in a down clue, the subordinate sits beneath the other piece
at the front picks out the first letter of the general's name

parts.note: a shot is a go, an attempt

explanation.surface: A soldier serving under General Eisenhower shot at the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the first-person pronoun beginning a sentence, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The ego is the self, the 'I' of psychology.

clue.text: Socialist dude embracing old british soldier

parts.note: a socialist or leftist is a red

indicators.note: the word for dude wraps around the following letter

parts.note: cat is slang for a cool guy, a dude

explanation.surface: A left-wing man hugging an old British soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embracing' puts O inside CAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoats were British soldiers, named for their scarlet uniform jackets.

clue.text: Bowler embarrassed about extra mostly

indicators.note: about means turned round, read backwards

parts.note: embarrassed people go red

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter is lost

parts.note: in cricket a bye is an extra, a run not scored off the bat

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler, red-faced over giving away extras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses RED to DER; 'mostly' cuts BYE to BY. Bowler suggests cricket, but here it is a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A derby is the American name for a bowler, the round hard felt hat.

clue.text: Lady who might pull a blade?

definitions.text: Lady who might pull a blade?

parts.words: Lady who might pull a blade?
parts.note: the surface suggests a woman drawing a knife, but the blade is the flat end of an oar

explanation.surface: A woman who might draw a knife.
explanation.definitionFit: A female rower pulls on oars, whose broad flat ends are called blades.
